**Reading map:** Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, *Mathematics for Machine Learning* (2020), Chapter 12 §12.4. All examples are newly authored.

## Motivation

A linear boundary in raw coordinates may be too restrictive. A kernel computes dot products in a feature space without always constructing its coordinates explicitly.

## Derivation and notation

$$
k(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol z)=\langle\phi(\boldsymbol x),\phi(\boldsymbol z)\rangle,\quad k_{\rm RBF}(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol z)=\exp(-\gamma\|\boldsymbol x-\boldsymbol z\|_2^2)
$$

Read this model together with the distributional, geometric or optimisation assumptions. An equation without its domain of validity is not a complete explanation.

## Apply it to our running example

For x=(1,1), z=(2,1), squared Euclidean distance is one. With gamma=0.5 the RBF kernel is exp(-0.5)≈0.6065; for identical vectors the value is 1. The kernel thus measures similarity in the chosen feature geometry.

## Constraints and interpretation

A valid SVM kernel must produce positive-semidefinite Gram matrices under appropriate conditions. Large gamma may overfit, while small gamma may oversmooth; tuning should use validation data.

## Your turn

What RBF kernel value do you obtain when two feature vectors are identical, regardless of gamma>0?
